extracted.intended_audience: trade_mark practitioners, patent_office applicants, and lawyers advising on registration and infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory legal guidance on the procedures, restrictions, and remedies under the Trade Marks Registration Act and related rules (opposition, assignment, register entries, infringement, criminal offences, renewal). Targets practical steps and substantive standards for registration and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition — notice and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of opposition must be sent (with a stamp of 1s) and be accompanied by a duplicate unstamped notice to be sent to the applicant; the grounds of the opposition are required to be stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice requires a stamp of 1s and must include the grounds. A duplicate unstamped copy will be forwarded to the applicant. See Trade Marks Forms and Instructions for form and particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's counter-statement timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: Within two months after receipt of the notice (or such further time as the comptroller may allow) the applicant may send a counter-statement in duplicate of the grounds on which he relies; failure to do so will be deemed abandonment of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-statement may follow Form X (see Instructions). Comptroller may extend time. Applicants who do not timely file are treated as having abandoned the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security for costs on opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant files a counter-statement, the comptroller shall furnish a copy to the opponent and require him to give security in such manner and to such amount as the comptroller may require for costs which may be awarded in respect of the opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If security is not given within fourteen days (or further time allowed) the opposition is deemed withdrawn. Security is to be by bond (see Instructions). Applicant may object to solvency of security per Instructions 33–34.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition — case deemed for Court determination
rubrics_metrics.description: If security for costs is duly given by the opponent, the comptroller shall inform the applicant and thereupon the case shall be deemed to stand for determination of the Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the case stands for Court determination, the applicant may be required to issue summons in the High Court and serve the comptroller with a copy bearing endorsement of service or acceptance of service (or the comptroller may require alternate proceedings). See Trade Marks Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must take proper proceedings or application abandoned
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the applicant fails to take the proper proceedings within the time allowed (non-receipt of notice by the comptroller is sufficient proof), the application will be deemed to be abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comptroller may deem abandonment; applicants should ensure timely initiation of Court proceedings (e.g., a summons) where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment/transmission only in connection with goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: A trade mark, when registered, shall be assigned and transmitted only in connexion with the goodwill of the business concerned in the particular trade mark, and shall be determinable with that goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory enactment confirms prior common-law principle: assignment of goodwill generally transfers trade marks as well (cases cited). The trade mark cannot be assigned independently of the related goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of assigning goodwill not strictly by deed
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of goodwill need not necessarily be in writing or by deed; neither the Act nor the Rules contain an express provision as to the manner in which goodwill with a trade mark is to be assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Form K asks for particulars 'e.g., by deed dated...' it is doubtful that a deed is strictly required under the Act; historical rules required a deed under earlier Acts but the present statute does not expressly do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for entry as proprietor — Form K and particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person becomes entitled by assignment, transmission, or operation of law to a registered trade mark he must request entry on the register on Form K stating name, address, description and particulars of the assignment/transmission and show it was in connection with goodwill for the relevant classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In case of bodies corporate an agent may sign; for firms a member or agent may sign. Statements in the request must be verified by statutory declaration (see Trade Marks Rules 34–38). Fees apply for first and additional marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller may refuse registration where conflicting claims exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several persons claim to be registered as proprietor of the same trade mark the comptroller may refuse to register any of them until their rights have been determined according to law, and may require or himself submit the claimants to the Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicting claims are generally submitted to the High Court by special case (Trade Marks Rules). If parties cannot agree the comptroller may settle the special case on payment of the prescribed fee (see Forms T).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction — identical marks for same goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The comptroller shall not register in respect of the same goods or description of goods a trade mark identical with one already on the register with respect to such goods or description of goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identical marks may be registered for different classes or even other goods of the same class in some circumstances (case law). The Court has limited repeated registrations of the same old mark historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction — marks nearly resembling registered marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The comptroller shall not register with respect to the same goods or description of goods a trade mark so nearly resembling a trade mark already on the register with respect to such goods or description as to be calculated to deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resemblance to marks whose registration has not been completed is immaterial. Cases illustrate that resemblance may be in design, depiction (e.g., hand positions), colour, or overall impression; registration refused where purchaser likely to be misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction — words/designs disentitled to protection
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall not be lawful to register as part of or in combination with a trade mark any words the exclusive use of which would, by reason of their being calculated to deceive or otherwise, be deemed disentitled to protection in a Court of Justice, or any scandalous design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers misrepresentative or scandalous matter; courts may impose terms. See also instructions for further restrictions (sects. 64, Instrs 29–31).

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks disentitled due to misrepresentation or fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is any misrepresentation in a trade mark, or where the trade itself is fraudulent, the Court will not protect the trade mark; false statements as to origin, quality, or substances employed disentitle the owner to protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: false statements on labels/tickets; use of the word 'patent' where no patent ever existed may disentitle owner to relief. See cases cited (Ford v. Foster, Pidding v. Holl, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may impose terms and award costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms may be imposed by the Court in relation to registration or relief; costs of the comptroller and litigation may be awarded in appropriate cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Whiteley's Trade Mark and remarks on costs in relevant case law (e.g., In re Orr Ewing's Trade Mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of ‘common to the trade’ marks (sect. 74)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comptroller may enter on the register, as an addition to any trade mark, particular device/word/figure common to the trade (old marks: devices etc. used before 13 Aug 1875; new marks: distinctive word(s) even if common to trade), subject to conditions and disclaimer of exclusive use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a term/symbol is common to a trade (examples in Instructions: 'best', 'charcoal', vine-leaves, grape clusters) it must be disclaimed in the application. A element used by more than three persons before the cutoff date is 'common to the trade'. Disclaimers must be entered on the application form and signed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer requirement for common elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must disclaim any right to exclusive use of the part of the mark common to the trade; a copy of the disclaimer shall be entered on the register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclaimer is to be written at foot or back of the Application Form and each additional representation, and signed by the applicant or his agent. See Instructions 19.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of registration as equivalent to public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be equivalent to public use of the trade mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration removes the previous need to prove actual public market use in an infringement action (Rodgers v. Nowill, McAndrew v. Bassett).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of registered proprietor — prima facie and conclusive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration is prima facie evidence of the registrant's right to exclusive use, and after five years from the date of registration is conclusive evidence of that right, subject to provisions of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During the first five years registration can be disputed by persons claiming as good or better title; after five years the register is conclusive but subject to Act-based grounds (e.g., mark not being a trade mark entitled to registration). Marks may be removed if they ought not to have been registered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered proprietor’s powers and equities
rubrics_metrics.description: By sect. 87 the registered proprietor has, subject to any rights appearing on the register, power absolutely to assign, grant licenses as to, and otherwise deal with the trade mark; equities may be enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where statutory powers exist, equitable rights or equities in respect of the mark can be enforced in appropriate litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to sue for infringement — registration prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: A person shall not be entitled to institute proceedings to prevent or to recover damages for infringement of a trade mark capable of being registered under this Act unless it has been registered in pursuance of this Act or a repealed enactment; for other trade marks in use before the cutoff date, registration or a certificate of refusal is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comptroller may grant a certificate that registration has been refused on request and payment of prescribed fee; certificate of refusal is prima facie evidence of refusal (sect. 96). Old marks require certificate of refusal or registration to sue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for infringement — injunctions and damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy for infringement of a trade mark is an action for injunction and damages, or criminal proceedings under the Merchandise Marks Act 1862.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At common law remedies included deceit actions; in equity injunctions were available. Plaintiff may elect account of profits instead of damages (exclusive choice). Criminal statute provides misdemeanor remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements plaintiff must prove in infringement action
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed the plaintiff must prove (1) the existence of the trade mark; (2) the imitation of the mark by the defendant so as to injure the plaintiff; and (3) that he has not delayed in coming to the Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration counts as existence (sect. 76). Imitation need only be sufficient to lead or be likely to lead purchasers to believe they are buying the plaintiff's goods; identity is not required. Prompt enforcement is essential to preserve the mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for proving imitation/likelihood of deception
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient to show that the defendant has imitated the plaintiff's mark so as to lead, or be likely to lead, purchasers to believe they were purchasing the goods of the plaintiff; resemblance need not deceive side-by-side comparison but must be calculated to mislead incautious purchasers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks used on goods of the same class as the registered mark are relevant. Case law cited provides examples of what constitutes likely deception (Lord Blackburn, Johnston v. Orr Ewing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptness and delay as a defence
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be no delay in coming to the Court; undue delay may bar relief because 'the very life of a trade mark depends upon the promptitude with which it is vindicated'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interlocutory injunctions may be moved for immediately; however some delay to obtain necessary evidence may be excused. Courts consider estoppel by acquiescence where plaintiff's delay benefits him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory relief, discovery and inspection powers
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory injunction may be granted; the plaintiff may obtain discovery of persons to whom defendant sold infringing goods; the Court has power to order inspection of property, manufacture, instruments, and articles related to the alleged counterfeit mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules cited: Judicature Act, R.S.C. orders on motion procedure, interrogatories (leave required except in fraud/breach of trust), Order L rules for inspection. Merchandise Marks Act s.21 gives power for inspection of manufacture/process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of profits as alternative remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful plaintiff may elect an account of profits instead of damages, but cannot obtain both; the account is limited to profits six years before commencement and to profits properly attributable to use of the plaintiff's trade mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An account may be available even where defendant submits, though at plaintiff's peril as to costs. See Cartier v. Carlisle and forms for orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of damages and requirement to prove special damage
rubrics_metrics.description: In jury trials, if infringement is proved plaintiff is entitled to nominal damages; if plaintiff takes inquiry as to damages, special damage must be proved to recover actual damages. Courts will not assume defendant’s sales would have been plaintiff’s sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure of damages is not simply the profit plaintiff might have made; proof of special damage required on inquiry (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal statutory and common-law defences enumerated
rubrics_metrics.description: Usual defences include (1) the mark is not a trade mark; (2) non-registration in case of new marks; (3) plaintiff is not the registered proprietor; (4) plaintiff is not owner of business and goodwill in the relevant classes; (5) delay/estoppel; (6) mark has become publici juris; (7) misrepresentation by plaintiff; (8) license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each defence has distinct facts and consequences: e.g., a license may be pleaded but cannot justify deceptive use that misleads the public. Non-registration bars damages actions for new marks; old marks rely on certificate of refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal offences under the Merchandise Marks Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone who, with intent to defraud or enable fraud, forges/counterfeits a trade mark, applies forged/counterfeited marks to chattels not of the denoted merchandiser, mis-describes articles, applies marks to things intended for trade, encloses articles with falsely marked packaging, attaches false labels, procures/abets such offences, commits a misdemeanor punishable by up to two years' imprisonment, hard labour, fine, and forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute creates multiple specific criminal acts (sects. 2–3 and others). Conviction leads to forfeiture of chattels, instruments, and related items. False pretences prosecutions may also apply where fraudulently inducing purchase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture on conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every person convicted of the misdemeanor forfeits to Her Majesty all chattels/articles to which the counterfeit mark was applied, instruments for applying such marks, and related things in his possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forfeiture covers goods, tools, labels, tickets, and similar items used in the counterfeit trade. This is in addition to criminal punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register of Trade Marks — contents and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: There shall be kept at the Patent Office a Register of Trade Marks wherein shall be entered the names and addresses of proprietors of registered trade marks, notifications of assignments and transmissions of trade marks, and such other matters as may be prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries include proprietor name/address at registration (Trade Marks Rules 30). Applications for alteration of address use Form M and incur a fee per mark. Register rectification procedures are available (see sect. 90).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and verification for assignments/transmissions
rubrics_metrics.description: When entitled by assignment/transmission/operation of law a person may apply to be registered by sending Form K with particulars showing how the mark became vested and that assignment/transmission was in connection with goodwill for the relevant class; statements must be verified by statutory declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees apply (1s for first mark, 25s for each additional mark transmitted at same time per Rules' schedule). Particulars differ in cases of death, bankruptcy, etc.; see notes to sect. 55 and Rules 34–39.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal and removal procedure at 14-year intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: Not less than two months nor more than three months before expiration of fourteen years from registration the comptroller shall send notice to the registered proprietor that the trade mark will be removed unless the proprietor pays the prescribed fee before expiration; a second notice is sent one month after the first if fee unpaid; if fee still unpaid the comptroller may remove the mark after three months from expiration and so at every 14-year interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proprietors must pay prescribed renewal fees at each fourteen-year period to avoid removal. Comptroller's notices specify dates and fees; removal is discretionary after notice period lapses.
